1.3 Electron configurations 
Line spectra 
Atoms absorb and emit energy in the form of electromagnetic radiation, often 
as visible light. For example, yellow street lamps centain sodium vapour that 
is excited by an electrical discharge and gives out light. If you put this light 
through a prism or aspectroscope, it will splitinto a series of coloured lines 
(figure 3). This is an emission spectrum. An absorption spectrum is seen when 
atoms absorb energy from a continuous spectrum of light, and it consists of a 
series of dark lines against a coloured background. The lines in the emission 
and absorption spectra of the same element have the same wavelengths. 
A Figure 3 A sodium lamp (top) and its emission spectrum (bottom) 
Approaches to learning 
It may help you to remember the principles of emission spectroscopy if you 
think about the colours observed in a fireworks display, or in flame tests. In 
fireworks, very fast redox reactions generate thermal energy. This energy 
excites atoms of metals, promoting electrons to higher energy levels. A 
promoted electron will stay in a higher level for a fraction of a second and 
then drop back down to a lower level, emitting a photon of light. The 
wavelength of this photon corresponds to the energy difference between 
the levels and is characteristic for the element (for example, lithium —red, 
sodium—yellow, barium—pale green, copper—blue-green). 
Absorption spectra and emission spectra provide evidence for the 
Bohr model of the atom, in which electrons travel around the nucleus in 
particular orbits with certain energies. The line emission spectrum of hydrogen 
is shown in figure 4, along with the corresponding electron transitions 
between the energy levels in the atom. When an electron falls from a higher 
to a lower energy level, a photon is emitted. The photon has a particular 
wavelength, A, which depends on the energy difference between the two levels.

Electron configurations 
The Bohr model assigns a number (n) to each energy level, with the lowest 
being n=1. Each energy level, or shell, can hold up to 2n? electrons. 
For example, the maximum numbers of electrons in the first, second and third 
energy levels are 2, 8 and 18, respectively. 
Energy levels split into sublevels, with as many sublevels as the value of n. 
The sublevels are s, p, d and f, of progressively higher energy. The first level, 
with n =1, contains only a single s-sublevel; the second level, with n = 2, 
contains s- and p-sublevels, and so on. 
* Anorbital is a region of space where there is a high probability of 
finding an electron. 
» Asublevel is a part of an energy level, made up of orbitals. 
* An electron configuration is a notation that describes the arrangement 
of electrons in the energy levels and sublevels of an atom. 
Each sublevel contains a fixed number of atomic orbitals. Each orbital 
has a certain energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical 
environment, and it can hold two electrons of opposite spin. 
The relationship between sublevels and atomic orbitals is shown in figure 5.

When working out electron configurations, remember the following: 
* label all energy levels and sublevels clearly 
* use the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity and the 
Pauli exclusion principle 
* inthe first row of the d-block elements, electrons occupy the 
3d sublevel, not 4d 
* atoms of chromium and copper in the ground state contain only 
one electron in the 4s sublevel, so their electron configurations are 
[Ar]3d®4s' and [Ar]3d'%4s', respectively 
* in cations, electrons are removed first from the energy level with the 
highest value of n. For example, the configuration of Fe** is [Ar]3d®, 
not [Ar]3d?4s? 
* The Aufbau principle states that electrons fill orbitals of the lowest 
available energy. 
¢ Hund'’s rule of maximum multiplicity states that, for orbitals of the 
same energy (degenerate orbitals), electrons fill the orbitals singly 
before pairing. 
* The Pauli exclusion principle states that any orbital has a maximum 
capacity of two electrons, and these electrons have opposite spins 
("up” and “down”).

Successive ionization energies increase as electrons are removed from 
increasingly positive species. However, this increase is not smooth because 
certain electron configurations are particularly stable. A large jump in value 
between IE_and IE_ means that the (x + 1)th electron has been removed 
from a lower energy level or sublevel, or from a half-filled sublevel. 
Example 6 
The first five successive ionization energies for an unknown transition 
element have the following values: 633, 1235, 2389, 7091 and 
8843k mol'. Deduce the group of the periodic table in which this element 
is likely to be found. 
Solution 
The largest difference in energy is observed between the third and the 
fourth values, so the fourth electron is likely to be removed from a lower 
energy level. Therefore, the outermost energy level of the element contains 
three electrons, so the element belongs to either group 3 or group 13. 
However, the question states that it is a transition element, so the only 
possible answer is group 3.

Example 7 
Explain, with reference to electron configuration, why the general increase in the first ionization energy across the 
third period is not observed for the following pairs of elements: 
a) from magnesium, Mg, to aluminium, Al 
b) from phosphorus, P, to sulfur, S 
Solution 
a) Inaluminium, the two paired 3s electrons shield the outermost 3p electron, making this electron slightly easier 
to remove and thus lowering the IE, value. Therefore, the IE, of aluminium (578 k) mol™') is lower than that of 
magnesium (738 k| mol-'). 
b) Insulfur, the two paired 3p electrons occupy the same orbital, which increases their mutual repulsion and thus lowers 
the energy required to remove one of these electrons. Therefore, the IE, of sulfur (1000 k mol™) is lower than that of 
phosphorus (1012k) mol).

Elements of each group of the periodic table generally have the same electron 
configuration for their outer energy levels. Going down a group, the atomic 
radius increases, so the outer electrons move further away from the nucleus. 
In addition, the shielding effect of the core electrons increases faster than the 
nuclear charge. Both factors reduce the ionization energy of heavier elements 
in comparison with their lighter analogues.
